title: Zetta: A Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence
hook: Most robot agents reflect only after the episode ends — too late to save it. Zetta writes and revises its own runtime critics mid-rollout, while the base policy stays frozen.
key_points: Existing embodied harnesses are open-loop: fixed skills during rollout, post-hoc reflection after it.
Physical interaction changes faster than a large agentic model can think, so governance has to happen at action frequency.
Zetta runs three timescale-separated loops: action-frequency governance, rollout-level critic/recovery proposals, validation-gated skill updates.
Critics and recovery skills are code the system evolves online; the base policy is never retrained.
Reports 90.8% on LIBERO-Pro and 93.6% on RoboCasa with an 11.1x inference speedup, and skills that transfer zero-shot.
content_html: End-to-end robot policies still leave a reliability gap, so people wrap them in agentic scaffolds. But those scaffolds are almost all open-loop: the agent picks from a fixed skill set during a rollout and only reflects once the episode is over. Zetta, from a team at Tsinghua and collaborators, argues that's the wrong shape — physical interaction demands decisions that track a fast-changing robot-environment state, at a frequency no large agentic model can hit directly.
extra_html:
How it works

Zetta keeps the base policy frozen and instead evolves code: runtime critics that watch execution and recovery skills that intervene. Three loops run at separated timescales — an action-frequency governance loop that can act inside a motion, a rollout-level loop that proposes new critics and recovery skills, and a slower loop that only commits a skill once validation confirms it. A companion infrastructure layer, Z-Infra, decouples the agent logic from whatever heterogeneous execution resources are actually available.

Why it matters

The authors report state-of-the-art success under their rollout budget — 90.8% on LIBERO-Pro and 93.6% on RoboCasa — alongside an 11.1x inference speedup, with performance that keeps climbing as the system accumulates self-exploration experience and learned skills that transfer zero-shot. The broader claim is a scaling axis: instead of scaling the policy, scale the harness's ability to improve itself.

related.title: SHAPER: Adapting Embodied Agents by Evolving Skills and Harness, Not Weights
related.hook: When a robot agent fails in a new environment, the reflex is to fine-tune. SHAPER freezes the model and instead evolves the skills and harness wrapped around it — no data, no rewards, no training run.

related.title: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Model
related.hook: π0 is a generalist robot policy: it takes camera images, joint angles, and a plain-language instruction, and outputs smooth action sequences — folding laundry, bussing tables, bagging groceries.

related.title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable
related.hook: An agent is only as good as its harness — the code that builds prompts, manages state, calls tools. The real bottleneck isn't editing that code, it's finding where a behavior lives in a huge codebase.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't post-episode reflection govern a robot's physical execution?
flashcards.back_html: Robot–environment state changes faster than a large agentic model can react. By the time the episode ends and reflection runs, the decisions that mattered have already been made.

flashcards.prompt: What does Zetta actually update online?

choices.text: Code-based runtime critics and recovery skills, while the base policy stays frozen
The weights of the base manipulation policy
The reward model used for offline fine-tuning

flashcards.explanation_html: Zetta evolves code — critics and recovery skills — and gates the updates on validation. The underlying policy is never retrained.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Zetta separate its three loops by timescale?

choices.text: Different decisions need different frequencies: per-action governance, per-rollout proposals, validated skill updates
To let three separate models be trained in parallel on different GPUs
Because the simulator only exposes state at three fixed rates

flashcards.explanation_html: Fast governance must run at action frequency; proposing new critics needs a whole rollout to judge; committing a skill needs validation. Splitting them lets each run at its natural rate.
